messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir was thirty years old, a tax inspector for the state, when his life fractured on a rain-slicked highway. He had been driving home late, exhausted after a week of field audits, when a drunk driver swerved across the median and struck his sedan head-on. The smell of alcohol—from the other driver’s breath as he leaned into Amir’s window, from the stale beer cans that rolled across the pavement—flooded the car. Amir survived with a broken collarbone and deep bruising, but the image of the other car, a blue sedan identical to his own, crumpled against the guardrail, never left him. In the months that followed, he could not be a passenger without his heart hammering; he could not walk past a parked car with a similar curve without seeing his own destruction. Every loud sound—a truck backfiring, a door slamming—sent him diving into a crouch, his chest tight with the certainty that another impact was coming.

The triggers multiplied. At his desk in the Department of Revenue, the faint whiff of hand sanitizer on a colleague’s hands would conjure the raw alcohol smell of the crash, and Amir would feel his stomach drop. A flash of blue in the parking lot outside his window made him freeze mid-sentence. Each time, the threat response surged: his eyes darted to exits, his neck prickled, he became convinced something terrible was about to happen. He started arriving late to work because he would circle the block three times to avoid passing a repair shop with a wrecked vehicle out front. The hypervigilance wore him down, and yet he couldn’t stop scanning the road, the hallway, the break room for signs of danger. What frightened him most was that the threat felt real even in safe places, and he had come to believe he could no longer trust his own instincts—the accident had proven he was not capable of protecting himself.

That belief hardened into a deeper conviction: he would never feel normal emotions again. Amir had always prided himself on being steady, reliable, someone who could handle the stress of audits and confrontations with taxpayers. Now, when he looked at his reflection, he saw a stranger who jumped at shadows and couldn’t sit through a meal without his throat closing. The negative appraisals gnawed at him: *I can’t rely on myself to keep safe, so I can’t rely on myself to do anything.* Those thoughts made every trigger more potent—because if he was fundamentally broken, then of course a car like that one meant death was near. Convinced that his own instincts had permanently failed him and he could not rely on himself to judge what was safe, Amir reasoned that the only rational way to stay alive was to eliminate any possible reminder of the crash from his daily life. He began to notice the blue sedan everywhere, convinced the universe was testing him, and each sighting reinforced his helplessness.

To cope, Amir developed strategies that slowly consumed his life. He stopped driving entirely, taking the bus to work—a route that forced him to walk past the very intersection where the crash had happened, but at least he wasn’t behind the wheel. To avoid the empty hours when memories ambushed him, he buried himself in his phone, scrolling through social media and playing puzzle games late into the night, until his eyes burned and he forgot to eat dinner. The undereating started as a side effect—he lost his appetite, his stomach knotted at the thought of food—but soon he realized it gave him a sense of control, a way to keep something small from spiraling. Yet each avoidance loop tightened the cycle: when he spent hours on screens instead of resting, he felt more disconnected, more convinced he was no longer capable of normal human functioning. And the more he avoided the world, the more his hypervigilance grew—because he never gave himself a chance to learn that a loud sound was just a truck, not a crash.

His marriage dissolved within a year. His wife had tried to be patient, but Amir could not sit in the passenger seat with her, could not go to restaurants where alcohol was served, could not even laugh at a joke without a haunted look crossing his face. She told him he had vanished inside himself, and she was right—he had. At work, his manager noticed he was requesting only office-based assignments, avoiding any audit that required a site visit. Amir knew he was shrinking his life, but every step felt necessary for survival.

What finally brought him to a clinic was a new trigger: a blue sedan identical to the one he had driven, parked in his boss’s spot. He spent the rest of the day in the bathroom, trembling, unable to breathe. He realized that if he did not get help, he would lose his job, his sanity, maybe his will to live. He was terrified of reliving the crash in therapy, of having to talk about the moment the glass shattered. But he was also terrified of staying the same—a man who could not rely on himself, who could not feel anything except the raw edge of fear. He came in hoping that somewhere inside him, the capable person he used to be was still there, waiting to be found.
